prompt: Write an essay of advice for a new PhD student on choosing a research problem. About 800 words. Output only the essay, with no title.
raw:
One of the most consequential decisions you will make in your PhD is not which experiments to run or which papers to write, but which problem to devote years of your life to. The choice of a research problem shapes your daily experience, your intellectual growth, your relationship with your advisor, and ultimately the trajectory of your career. It deserves careful thought, but not paralysis. Here is what I wish someone had told me when I was starting.

First, understand that choosing a problem is not a single event but a process. You will likely refine your question multiple times before settling into the work that becomes your dissertation. This is normal and healthy. Early in your program, give yourself permission to explore broadly. Read outside your immediate subfield. Attend seminars that seem only tangentially related. Talk to people whose work you admire and ask them not just what they do but why they chose it. The goal in these early months is to build a landscape of possibilities in your mind, so that when you do commit, you do so with some awareness of what you are choosing over.

That said, do not let exploration become indefinite delay. There is a real cost to waiting too long to commit. Research problems reveal their character only through sustained engagement, and you cannot learn whether a problem is right for you by thinking about it from the outside. Set yourself a rough timeline—six months to a year of active exploration, depending on your field—and then make a decision you can revise later if needed.

When you are evaluating potential problems, resist the temptation to choose based solely on prestige or perceived importance. The most famous open problems in your field may be famous precisely because they are extraordinarily difficult, or because they require tools and insights that do not yet exist. Working on such a problem can be exhilarating, but it can also be isolating and demoralizing if you make little progress for years. A better heuristic is to look for problems that are important enough to matter but tractable enough that a single person, working for several years with the resources available to them, can make genuine progress. The sweet spot is often found at the intersection of a significant question and a methodological gap—a place where existing approaches have been exhausted but new ones are within reach.

Equally important is your personal relationship to the problem. You will spend thousands of hours thinking about it, often in states of confusion and frustration. If the question does not genuinely interest you—if you are pursuing it only because your advisor suggested it or because it seems strategic—you will find it very difficult to sustain the effort required when things get hard. This does not mean you need to feel passionate about it from day one. Interest can grow through understanding. But there should be some seed of curiosity, some sense that you want to know the answer for its own sake.

Your advisor's role in this process is significant but complicated. A good advisor can help you identify problems that are well-suited to your skills and stage of development, and they can warn you away from dead ends they have already explored. But be cautious about simply adopting your advisor's problem wholesale. You need to develop your own intellectual identity, and that is much harder if your research agenda is entirely someone else's. Aim for a problem that sits within your advisor's broader program but that you can claim as your own—a question they care about but that you will pursue in your own way.

Pay attention to the social dimensions of your choice as well. Research is increasingly collaborative, and the problem you choose determines the community you will be part of. Consider whether the people working on related questions are generous, rigorous, and welcoming. A supportive intellectual community can make an otherwise difficult problem feel manageable, while a toxic or competitive one can poison even the most elegant research question.

Finally, accept that you will not choose perfectly. Every problem has hidden difficulties, and every choice involves tradeoffs you cannot fully anticipate. The students who thrive are not those who pick the optimal problem on their first try, but those who learn to adapt—to narrow their scope when a problem proves too large, to pivot when a dead end becomes clear, to find unexpected value in results that differ from what they hoped for. Choosing a research problem is an exercise in judgment under uncertainty, and like all such exercises, it improves with practice. Give yourself grace, stay curious, and trust that the work of figuring out what to study is itself a form of learning.
